disease.name: Diabetes Mellitus

overview.description: Diabetes Mellitus is a group of chronic metabolic diseases characterized by high blood glucose (hyperglycemia) resulting from defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both. Insulin is a hormone produced by the pancreas that allows sugar (glucose) from food to enter cells and be used for energy.
overview.affected_organ: Pancreas (primary), also affects kidneys, eyes, nerves, heart, and blood vessels
overview.prevalence: Approximately 537 million adults affected worldwide (IDF, 2023); 77 million in India alone
overview.age_group: All age groups; Type 1 common in children; Type 2 more common in adults 40+

types.name: Type 1 Diabetes (T1D)
types.description: An autoimmune condition where the immune system destroys insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. Little to no insulin is produced. Requires lifelong insulin therapy.
types.cause: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells

types.name: Type 2 Diabetes (T2D)
types.description: The body either doesn't produce enough insulin or doesn't use it effectively (insulin resistance). Most common type. Strongly linked to lifestyle factors.
types.common_in: Adults over 40; increasingly seen in younger populations due to obesity
types.cause: Insulin resistance + progressive beta cell dysfunction

types.name: Gestational Diabetes (GDM)
types.description: Diabetes that develops during pregnancy in women who didn't have diabetes before. Usually resolves after delivery but increases risk of Type 2 later.

types.name: MODY (Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young)
types.description: A rare monogenic form caused by single-gene mutations. Diagnosed in adolescents and young adults.
types.common_in: Young adults under 25 with strong family history
types.cause: Single gene mutations affecting insulin secretion

types.name: LADA (Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults)
types.description: A slow-progressing form of autoimmune diabetes that begins in adulthood. Often misdiagnosed as Type 2.
types.cause: Autoimmune (similar to Type 1 but slower progression)

types.name: Prediabetes
types.description: Blood sugar levels are higher than normal but not high enough for a diabetes diagnosis. Highly reversible with lifestyle changes.

types.name: Secondary Diabetes
types.description: Diabetes caused by other conditions or medications.

type1_causes: Autoimmune destruction of beta cells (T-cell mediated)
Early exposure to cow's milk proteins (possible trigger)
type2_causes: Obesity and excess body fat (especially abdominal/visceral fat)
Unhealthy diet high in refined carbohydrates and sugar
Insulin resistance in muscle, liver, and fat cells
Ethnicity (South Asians, Africans, Hispanics have higher risk)
Chronic stress and high cortisol levels

risk_factors: HDL cholesterol < 35 mg/dL or triglycerides > 250 mg/dL
PCOS or other insulin resistance syndromes
History of gestational diabetes or baby > 4 kg at birth
Chronic use of corticosteroids, antipsychotics, or thiazides

classic_symptoms.name: Polyuria (Frequent Urination)
classic_symptoms.description: Excess glucose in blood causes kidneys to work harder, pulling more water and resulting in frequent urination.

classic_symptoms.name: Polydipsia (Excessive Thirst)
classic_symptoms.description: Increased urination causes dehydration, leading to intense thirst.

classic_symptoms.name: Polyphagia (Excessive Hunger)
classic_symptoms.description: Cells cannot use glucose for energy properly, causing constant hunger despite eating.

classic_symptoms.name: Unexplained Weight Loss
classic_symptoms.description: Body breaks down fat and muscle for energy when glucose cannot enter cells.

classic_symptoms.name: Fatigue and Weakness
classic_symptoms.description: Cells starved of glucose energy leads to persistent tiredness.

classic_symptoms.name: Blurred Vision
classic_symptoms.description: High blood sugar causes fluid to be pulled from the eye lens, affecting ability to focus.

classic_symptoms.name: Slow Healing Wounds
classic_symptoms.description: High glucose impairs blood flow and immune function, delaying wound healing.

classic_symptoms.name: Frequent Infections
classic_symptoms.description: High glucose weakens immune system; common infections include UTIs, skin, and yeast infections.

secondary_symptoms: Tingling, numbness, or burning sensation in hands and feet (neuropathy)
Darkening of skin in body creases (Acanthosis Nigricans — insulin resistance sign)
Recurrent gum disease or dental infections
Itchy skin, especially in groin area
Fruity-smelling breath (sign of DKA in Type 1)
type1_specific_symptoms: Rapid onset over days to weeks
Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) — nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fruity breath
type2_specific_symptoms: Discovered incidentally on routine blood tests
Acanthosis Nigricans (dark patches on neck, armpits, groin)

emergency_symptoms.action: Consume 15g fast-acting carbs (glucose tablets, juice, sugar). Recheck after 15 minutes. Seek help if no improvement.
MEDICAL EMERGENCY. Call emergency services immediately. Requires IV fluids, insulin, and electrolyte replacement.
MEDICAL EMERGENCY. Requires hospital admission and IV fluid resuscitation.

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Diet is one of the most powerful tools in diabetes management. The right diet helps control blood sugar, body weight, blood pressure, and cholesterol — all critical in diabetes.
key_dietary_principles: Choose low Glycemic Index (GI) foods that release glucose slowly
Control portion sizes to avoid blood sugar spikes
Eat at regular intervals — do not skip meals
Limit refined carbohydrates, sugar, and processed foods
Choose healthy fats over saturated and trans fats
Limit sodium (salt) intake for blood pressure control
Stay well hydrated with water and unsweetened beverages
Alcohol should be consumed only with caution and doctor approval

sample_meal_plan.note: This is a general guideline for a ~1600-1800 kcal diabetic diet. Individual needs vary. Consult a registered dietitian.
sample_meal_plan.early_morning_pre_breakfast: 2 soaked almonds + 5 soaked fenugreek seeds swallowed with water OR 1 glass warm cinnamon water
sample_meal_plan.breakfast: 1 cup steel-cut oats with chia seeds and berries OR 2 whole wheat rotis + 1 bowl moong dal + 1 glass buttermilk
sample_meal_plan.mid_morning: 1 small apple or guava OR 1 cup green tea (no sugar)
sample_meal_plan.lunch: 1-2 brown rice cups + 1 bowl sambar (with lots of vegetables) + cucumber and tomato salad + 1 bowl plain curd
sample_meal_plan.afternoon_snack: 1 small handful of mixed nuts (almonds, walnuts) + 1 cup green tea OR 1 bowl sprouts salad
sample_meal_plan.dinner: 2 multigrain rotis + 1 bowl rajma/chana OR grilled fish + stir-fried vegetables (spinach, broccoli, capsicum) + 1 bowl dal
sample_meal_plan.if_hungry_before_bed: 1 glass warm low-fat milk with a pinch of turmeric (if blood sugar is stable)

recommended_exercises.intensity: Moderate intensity (can talk but slightly breathless)

recommended_exercises.benefit: Builds muscle mass; improves insulin sensitivity significantly
Reduces stress; improves balance (important to prevent falls in diabetic neuropathy)

precautions: Check blood sugar before and after exercise
If blood sugar < 100 mg/dL before exercise, have a small snack first
If blood sugar > 250 mg/dL and ketones present, avoid vigorous exercise
Wear proper footwear — diabetic foot care is essential
Inspect feet before and after exercise

weight_management: Even 5-10% body weight loss significantly improves blood sugar control
Caloric deficit of 500-750 kcal/day for safe weight loss
Combine diet and exercise for best results
Avoid crash diets or extreme food restriction

frequency.type1: 4-10 times per day or continuous CGM
frequency.gestational: 4 times daily (fasting + 1 hour after each meal)

blood_sugar_monitoring.log_and_share: Record readings in a diary or app; share with doctor at every visit

stress_management: Stress hormones (cortisol, adrenaline) raise blood sugar
Practice mindfulness meditation, deep breathing, or progressive muscle relaxation daily
Yoga is particularly beneficial for both stress and blood sugar management
Maintain a regular sleep schedule (7-9 hours per night)
Seek counseling or therapy if anxiety or depression is present (common in diabetes)

foot_care.importance: Diabetic neuropathy and poor circulation make feet vulnerable to ulcers, infections, and amputation
daily_care: Inspect feet daily for cuts, blisters, redness, or swelling
Wash feet daily with mild soap and lukewarm water; dry thoroughly between toes
Moisturize feet (not between toes) to prevent dryness and cracking
Trim toenails straight across; do not cut too short
Wear well-fitting, comfortable shoes with socks at all times
Avoid heating pads or hot water bottles on feet
See a podiatrist if any wound, ulcer, or infection develops

dental_care: Diabetes increases risk of gum disease (periodontitis)
Brush teeth twice daily with fluoride toothpaste
lifestyle_management.smoking_cessation: Smoking dramatically increases risk of heart attack, stroke, and kidney disease in diabetes. Quitting is the single most impactful lifestyle change alongside blood sugar control.

complications.overview: Poorly managed diabetes causes damage to blood vessels and nerves throughout the body over time.

microvascular.description: Damage to blood vessels in the retina; leading cause of blindness in working-age adults
microvascular.prevention: Tight glucose and BP control; annual dilated eye exam

microvascular.description: Progressive kidney damage leading to chronic kidney disease and potentially end-stage renal failure
microvascular.prevention: Control glucose, BP (use ACE inhibitor/ARB), limit protein in diet

microvascular.description: Nerve damage causing numbness, tingling, pain (peripheral), or autonomic dysfunction (gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, orthostatic hypotension)
microvascular.prevention: Strict glucose control; B12 supplementation if on metformin

macrovascular.description: 2-4x higher risk; largest cause of death in Type 2 diabetes
macrovascular.prevention: Glucose + BP + cholesterol control; statins; aspirin; smoking cessation

macrovascular.description: 2-3x higher risk due to damaged blood vessels in brain
Narrowed blood vessels in legs causing pain, poor wound healing, and risk of amputation
macrovascular.prevention: Exercise; glucose control; smoking cessation; statins

other_complications.description: Combination of neuropathy and PAD leads to non-healing ulcers and gangrene
Fat accumulation in liver; closely linked to insulin resistance
High glucose impairs immune function; higher risk of TB, UTI, skin, and fungal infections

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can Type 2 diabetes be reversed?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Type 2 diabetes can go into remission (HbA1c below 6.5% without medication) through significant weight loss (10-15% of body weight) and sustained lifestyle changes. This is most achievable in the early years after diagnosis. However, it requires permanent lifestyle maintenance to sustain.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is diabetes hereditary?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Both Type 1 and Type 2 have genetic components. Type 2 has a stronger hereditary link — if both parents have Type 2, a child has a 50-70% lifetime risk. However, lifestyle choices play a major role and can prevent or delay onset even in high-risk individuals.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can I eat rice and roti with diabetes?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes, but in controlled portions and preferably in the whole-grain form. Brown rice, millets, and whole wheat roti are better choices. Pair with high-fiber vegetables and protein to slow glucose absorption. Portion control is key.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is HbA1c and how often should it be tested?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: HbA1c (glycated hemoglobin) reflects your average blood sugar over the past 2-3 months. A result of 6.5% or above confirms diabetes. For managed diabetes, the goal is generally below 7%. Test every 3 months if not at target, or every 6 months when well-controlled.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can diabetics eat fruits?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes, but choose low GI fruits like guava, jamun, apple, pear, and berries. Avoid high-sugar fruits like mango, banana, grapes, and litchi in large portions. Always eat whole fruit rather than juice, as the fiber slows glucose absorption.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is insulin the last resort for Type 2 diabetes?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: No — insulin is a very effective medication, not a sign of failure. Some patients with Type 2 may need insulin early, especially if blood sugar is very high at diagnosis. Starting insulin early can preserve pancreatic function and prevent complications.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Type 1 is autoimmune — the body destroys insulin-producing cells and produces no insulin; it requires lifelong insulin. Type 2 is mainly lifestyle-related — the body produces insulin but doesn't use it effectively; it is managed with lifestyle, oral medications, and sometimes insulin.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can I exercise safely with diabetes?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes, and it is strongly recommended. Exercise is one of the most powerful tools for blood sugar control. Always check blood sugar before and after exercise, carry a fast-acting glucose source, wear proper footwear, and consult your doctor before starting a new exercise program.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How do I treat hypoglycemia (low blood sugar)?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Follow the 15-15 rule: consume 15g of fast-acting carbohydrates (glucose tablets, 1/2 cup juice, or sugar in water), wait 15 minutes, and recheck blood sugar. Repeat if still below 70 mg/dL. If unconscious, give glucagon injection or call emergency services.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Does stress affect blood sugar?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes. Physical and emotional stress releases hormones like cortisol and adrenaline that raise blood sugar. Managing stress through yoga, meditation, sleep, and exercise is an important part of diabetes management.
